passage: When Amandeep's grandfather died, the whole village came to the house. Ojas, his friend from the next lane, stood near the gate, unsure whether to go in. He'd known Bauji since he was small; the old man used to give them sugarcane from his field. Inside, Amandeep sat very still, eyes dry, while women sang and neighbours brought food. Ojas sat beside him and said nothing. After the cremation, Amandeep finally spoke. "I didn't even cry. Is something wrong with me?" Ojas shook his head. A week later they walked to the sugarcane field, and Amandeep cut a stalk and suddenly sat down in the mud and cried for a long time. Ojas stayed until he stood up.

qa.q: What did Bauji use to give the boys?
qa.a: He used to give them sugarcane from his field.

qa.q: Why did Amandeep ask if something was wrong with him?
qa.a: He felt confused and maybe guilty that he hadn't cried at the funeral, as if his grief didn't look the way it should.

qa.q: What did Ojas get right in supporting Amandeep?
qa.a: He stayed close, didn't force him to talk or cry, and was there when the grief finally came out in the field.

qa.q: Why might the field bring out Amandeep's tears when the funeral didn't?
qa.a: The field was full of personal memories of Bauji, while the crowded funeral may have felt too formal or overwhelming to grieve freely.

grounding: It shows a teen facing his first loss, grieving in his own time, supported by a friend.

passage: Camila's dog, Pepa, died on a rainy Tuesday in Lima. She was fourteen and had had Pepa since she was four. At school she said nothing. She didn't want to be the girl crying about a dog. Her friend Gabriel noticed she didn't eat lunch. "Is it Pepa?" he asked quietly. He had walked the dog with her twice. Camila's throat closed. She nodded. "Everyone says it's just a pet." Gabriel shrugged. "She was yours for ten years. That's not just." That weekend Camila made a small album of Pepa's photos. Gabriel came over and they looked at it together, laughing at one with Pepa wearing a paper hat. Camila cried and laughed at the same time. It felt strange but okay.

qa.q: How long had Camila had Pepa?
qa.a: She had Pepa since she was four, about ten years.

qa.q: Why did Camila say nothing at school at first?
qa.a: She feared people would think her grief over a dog was silly and didn't want to be seen crying about it.

qa.q: How did Gabriel's words help Camila?
qa.a: By saying ten years together was not "just" a pet, he validated her sadness and made it easier for her to open up.

qa.q: How might Gabriel feel looking at the album with Camila?
qa.a: He probably felt sad too, since he had walked Pepa, but also glad to be trusted with Camila's memories. 🤍

grounding: It shows a teen grieving her first pet and finding a way to mourn with a friend's support.

passage: In Class 10, Gopika's classmate died in a road accident during the summer holidays. When school reopened, his desk stood empty near the window. Nobody sat there. The teachers said a few words at assembly, then lessons went on. Gopika felt strange, angry that everything was normal. Her friend Manjula found her in the library one lunch break, not reading. "I keep looking at his desk," Gopika said. The school counsellor had put up a notice about a remembrance corner. Manjula said, "Let's write something there." They each wrote a note: Gopika about how he always lent her pencils, Manjula about his terrible jokes. Other students added notes over the week. Gopika still looked at the desk, but it felt a little less empty.

qa.q: What did Gopika write in her note about her classmate?
qa.a: She wrote about how he always lent her pencils.

qa.q: Why did Gopika feel angry when lessons went on?
qa.a: It felt wrong to her that life at school seemed normal when her classmate was gone, as if his absence wasn't being honoured.

qa.q: How did the remembrance corner help the students grieve?
qa.a: It gave them a shared, safe place to put their memories into words, so the loss was recognised together.

qa.q: How might Manjula be feeling in this situation?
qa.a: Manjula is probably grieving too, and suggesting the notes was a way to support Gopika and share that grief at once.

grounding: It shows teens facing the loss of a classmate and finding a shared way to mourn at school.

passage:
Dear Yusuf,
You asked how I'm doing since Ammamma died. Honestly, I don't know. It's been three weeks. Some days I'm fine and then I hear a pressure cooker whistle and I cry because she always shouted 'Reena, turn it off!' Isn't that silly?
Amma gave me her green shawl. I sleep with it. It still smells of her coconut oil.
On Sunday, I tried making her tomato rasam from memory. It was too sour, and Appa laughed, and then he cried too. We sat in the kitchen together for a long time. That helped more than anything.
I've started writing down her sayings in a notebook so I don't forget.
Write back soon. Tell me about your new school.
Reena

qa.q: What did Amma give Reena that belonged to Ammamma?
qa.a: Her green shawl, which still smells of her coconut oil.

qa.q: Why did Reena cry when she heard a pressure cooker whistle?
qa.a: It reminded Reena of Ammamma shouting 'Reena, turn it off!', bringing the loss back suddenly.

qa.q: Which of Reena's ways of mourning could help other grieving teens?
qa.a: Keeping a meaningful object, cooking a family recipe and writing down the person's sayings.

qa.q: How might Appa have felt in the kitchen after laughing at the rasam?
qa.a: He was grieving Ammamma too, and sharing the moment with Reena let his own tears come.

grounding: A teen writes about grieving a grandmother and the ways the family mourns.

passage: You know how everyone says 'it was just a cat'? Mitthu wasn't just a cat to me. I'm Preeti, I'm sixteen, and I had him since I was seven. Last month he got sick and the vet said he was very old. My brother Vijay and I sat with him on the balcony till the end. After that, I didn't want to talk to anyone. At school a girl said, 'Get a new one,' and I wanted to scream. What helped? Vijay and I buried him under the neem tree and planted marigolds. I made a small photo album. And I let myself cry in the shower without feeling stupid. It's still sore, but lighter. I talk to him sometimes. Is that weird?

qa.q: Where did Preeti and Vijay bury Mitthu?
qa.a: Under the neem tree, where they planted marigolds.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel when a girl told her to 'get a new one'?
qa.a: Preeti was angry and hurt, because the comment dismissed how much Mitthu meant.

qa.q: What helped Preeti mourn in a healthy way?
qa.a: Burying him with a small ritual, making a photo album and allowing tears without shame.

qa.q: If you were the girl who said 'Get a new one', what would a kinder response have been?
qa.a: Saying 'I'm sorry, you had him for so long' would acknowledge that Preeti's grief was real.

grounding: A teen tells how they grieved a pet and found ways to mourn.

passage:
I'm Omkar, Kalyani's brother. When our Nani died in October, Kalyani, fifteen, didn't cry at the funeral. Everyone said she was strong.
But after that, she stopped eating dinner with us. She kept Nani's grey shawl on her bed and slept wrapped in it. Some nights I heard her talking softly, as if to someone.
One Sunday, Amma found her in the garden, planting a tulsi cutting from Nani's old pot. Kalyani said, “Nani watered this every morning. Someone has to.”
Amma knelt beside her, and they both cried then, finally.
Now every morning Kalyani waters the plant before school. I don't know what she says to it. But she eats dinner with us again.

qa.q: What did Kalyani plant in the garden?
qa.a: A tulsi cutting from Nani's old pot.

qa.q: How was Kalyani feeling in the weeks after the funeral?
qa.a: She was grieving deeply and quietly, missing Nani even though she didn't cry at first.

qa.q: What helped Kalyani begin to mourn?
qa.a: Planting and caring for Nani's tulsi gave her a way to remember Nani and let her finally cry with Amma.

qa.q: How might Amma feel crying with Kalyani in the garden?
qa.a: She probably feels sad but closer to her daughter, sharing their grief at last 🤍

grounding: A brother observes his sister's quiet grief for their grandmother and how she finds a way to mourn.

passage:
Tuesday: Zubin, the old brown dog Joseph, fourteen, had grown up with, didn't wake up. Joseph sat by the basket all morning and wouldn't go to school. He didn't speak all day.
The next Sunday: Joseph found Zubin's red collar behind the sofa. He held it and cried so hard his mother came running. She sat and cried with him.
A month later: Joseph made a small photo book: Zubin as a puppy, Zubin stealing chapatis, Zubin asleep on his school bag. He and his father planted a guava tree in the corner of the yard where Zubin used to lie in the sun.
Joseph still misses him. But he can talk about him now and laugh at the chapati stories.

qa.q: What did Joseph find behind the sofa?
qa.a: Zubin's red collar.

qa.q: How did Joseph feel when he found the collar?
qa.a: He felt overwhelming sadness and grief, crying very hard.

qa.q: What helped Joseph mourn Zubin?
qa.a: Crying with his mother, making a photo book and planting a tree with his father gave him ways to remember.

qa.q: How might Joseph's parents feel watching him grieve?
qa.a: They probably feel sad too, but glad they can share his grief and help him remember.

grounding: Over a month a fourteen-year-old grieves his dog and finds ways to mourn.

passage:
Minakshi, come, sit by your Pooja Dadi. I know you haven't slept since your classmate's funeral. Let me tell you something.
When I was sixteen, my best friend Shobha died of a fever. One week she was laughing with me by the well, and the next she was gone. I stopped talking. I wouldn't eat.
My mother didn't tell me to be brave. She gave me a notebook and said, “Write to her.”
So I did. Every night for a year. I told Shobha everything: exams, a boy I liked, my fights with my sister.
On the first anniversary I went to Shobha's mother, gave her the notebook and helped her cook for the prayer. She held me for a long time. Grief doesn't vanish, beti. It just finds a place to live.

qa.q: What did Pooja's mother give her?
qa.a: A notebook.

qa.q: How did young Pooja feel after Shobha died?
qa.a: She felt deep grief and shock, so heavy she stopped talking and eating.

qa.q: What choices in the story helped Pooja mourn?
qa.a: Writing to Shobha every night and later going to help Shobha's mother on the anniversary.

qa.q: How might Shobha's mother have felt when Pooja gave her the notebook?
qa.a: She probably felt moved and comforted to know how much her daughter was loved.

grounding: A grandmother shares how she mourned her best friend at sixteen, offering her grieving granddaughter a way to mourn.

passage:
Lavanya's grandmother died two days before her board exam. The house was full of relatives, the rituals went on until late, and there was nowhere quiet to study.
Lavanya sat on the stairs with her notes, not reading. Every time she looked at Paati's chair, her throat closed.
Nandini came over with her own textbook. "Want to study at mine? Or just sit?"
"I can't even cry. Everyone else is crying."
"You don't have to cry on a schedule."
They sat on Nandini's terrace. Lavanya read a page, then told Nandini about the way Paati used to hum while plaiting her hair. Then she cried, finally.
Her mother came to fetch her later and held her for a long time. "Paati would want you to write that exam. And to miss her too."

qa.q: What did Paati use to do while plaiting Lavanya's hair?
qa.a: Hum.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling when she said she couldn't even cry?
qa.a: Lavanya felt numb and confused by her grief, with the pressure of exams on top.

qa.q: What did Nandini do that helped Lavanya grieve?
qa.a: She offered a quiet place and simply listened, without telling Lavanya how or when to feel.

qa.q: How might Lavanya's mother be feeling when she holds her?
qa.a: Her mother is grieving too, but wants to comfort Lavanya and support her through the exam 🤍.

grounding: A teen grieves her grandmother amid exam pressure and a friend's quiet support.

passage:
For eleven years, Bruno the dog had slept at the foot of Sangeeta's bed in their Chennai flat. Last Sunday, he didn't wake up.
Sangeeta didn't go to school on Monday. She kept his lead in her hand and wouldn't let anyone put it away.
Her brother Yogesh sat with her. "Want to do something for him?"
They printed photos: Bruno as a puppy, Bruno stealing a dosa, Bruno asleep on Sangeeta's feet. They made a small album and wrote under each one.
In the evening, they planted a tulsi in Bruno's favourite corner of the balcony.
Sangeeta still cried at night. But she put the lead in a box with the album. "So I know where he is."

qa.q: How many years had Bruno slept at the foot of Sangeeta's bed?
qa.a: Eleven years.

qa.q: What does Sangeeta holding the lead suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: Sangeeta felt deep grief and wasn't ready to let go of Bruno.

qa.q: What way of mourning did Yogesh offer, and why did it help?
qa.a: Making an album and planting a tulsi gave Sangeeta a way to remember Bruno and express her grief.

qa.q: How might Yogesh be feeling while he helps Sangeeta?
qa.a: Yogesh probably misses Bruno too, and finds comfort in doing something together.

grounding: A teen mourns her dog with her brother's help through an album and a planting.

passage:
"It's a year today," said Mridul, looking at the cricket ground.
Lavanya nodded. "Since Arun."
"I still expect him to walk up and steal my bat."
"Me too. I texted his old number last week. By mistake." Lavanya laughed, then stopped.
"Do you think it gets easier?"
"It gets… different. Some days I forget, and then I feel guilty for forgetting."
Mridul picked at the grass. "His mum asked if we'd come today. They're putting a bench here."
"Will you come?"
"Only if you do."
Later, they sat on the new bench with Arun's parents. His mother held both their hands. Nobody said much.

qa.q: What were Arun's parents putting at the cricket ground?
qa.a: A bench.

qa.q: What was Lavanya feeling when she laughed, then stopped?
qa.a: Lavanya felt a flash of the old closeness and then sadness and guilt, remembering Arun was gone.

qa.q: How can friends support each other on an anniversary like this?
qa.a: By talking openly about the person, going to a memorial together, and accepting that grief changes rather than ends.

qa.q: How might Arun's mother feel when Mridul and Lavanya come?
qa.a: Arun's mother likely feels comforted 🤍 that his friends still remember him.

grounding: Two teens mark the anniversary of a friend's death together.

passage:
At Nani's funeral I didn't cry. Everyone else did. Aunties kept hugging me and I just stood there, feeling like a statue, and then feeling guilty for not crying.
Three weeks later I went into her room to find a pen. Her sewing machine was still open, with blue thread on it, the blouse she'd been stitching for me half-done. And then I couldn't stop. I sat on the floor for an hour.
Parveen came over that evening. She didn't say "she's in a better place". She just sat next to me and asked, "What was she like when she was annoyed?" And I laughed, because Nani used to scold the pressure cooker.
I finished the blouse myself last month, badly. I wear it anyway. I'm Madhuri, and I think grief doesn't come on time.

qa.q: What was still on Nani's sewing machine?
qa.a: Blue thread, and the blouse she'd been stitching, half-done.

qa.q: Why did Madhuri feel guilty at the funeral?
qa.a: Madhuri felt numb, like a statue, and guilty for not crying when everyone else did.

qa.q: What did Parveen do that helped, and why?
qa.a: Parveen sat with Madhuri and asked a question that let happy memories come up, instead of offering empty comfort.

qa.q: How might Parveen have felt sitting with a grieving friend?
qa.a: Parveen may have felt unsure what to say, but caring enough to stay and listen.

grounding: Shows a teen's delayed grief for a grandparent and finding a personal way to mourn.

passage:
Teacher's note. Kavitha, Class 9 class teacher.
Nandini has been very quiet this week. She usually argues with me about everything. Today she put her head down in the free period. When I asked quietly, she said her dog, Bruno, died on Sunday. He was fourteen, older than her.
She said, "It's silly, he's just a dog," and her eyes filled up.
I told her it wasn't silly at all; he'd been part of her family her whole life. I offered her some paper and suggested she write to him, or about him, if she wanted. She wrote for the whole period and asked to keep it.
I've informed her parents about how she's doing, and let her know the counsellor is there on Thursdays if she'd like to talk. I'll check in with her again on Monday.

qa.q: How old was Bruno when he died?
qa.a: Bruno was fourteen, older than Nandini.

qa.q: What does Nandini calling it "silly" while her eyes filled up suggest?
qa.a: It suggests Nandini felt deep grief but also embarrassed about feeling so sad over a pet.

qa.q: What did Kavitha do that other teachers could learn from?
qa.a: She took the loss seriously, offered a simple way to express it, told the parents and pointed to the counsellor, with a planned check-in.

qa.q: How might Nandini's parents feel when Kavitha tells them how she is doing?
qa.a: They may feel worried for their daughter but grateful that her teacher noticed her grief and took it seriously.

grounding: Illustrates a teacher supporting a teen's first loss of a pet and offering ways to mourn.

passage:
Sunday
Diary, Shreya here. Today was the thirteenth-day prayer for Nana. The house was full of people and incense.
In the afternoon my cousin Hemant and I hid on the terrace and started laughing about how Nana used to fall asleep during cricket and then insist he'd been watching. We laughed so hard. Then I felt terrible. Is it wrong to laugh when he's gone?
Mami found us. I thought she'd scold us. She sat down and said, "He'd want you laughing about him. That's how he stays."
So Hemant and I asked if we could plant a hibiscus by the gate, the red kind Nana always picked for his puja. We did it before sunset. My hands were muddy and I cried a bit.
It feels a little easier tonight.

qa.q: What did Shreya and Hemant plant by the gate?
qa.a: A red hibiscus, the kind Nana always picked for his puja.

qa.q: Why did Shreya feel terrible after laughing?
qa.a: Shreya felt guilty, worried that laughing so soon after Nana's death was disrespectful.

qa.q: How did planting the hibiscus help Shreya mourn?
qa.a: It gave Shreya something to do that honoured Nana, so the sadness had a place to go.

qa.q: How might Mami be feeling while comforting the two children?
qa.a: Mami is probably grieving too, but finds comfort in sharing happy memories and helping them grieve.

grounding: Shows a teen grieving a grandfather and finding ways to mourn, including laughter and a small ritual.
